title: Needs vs wants
summary: Sort spending in a way that fits your life, not someone else's rulebook.

sections.heading: There is no universal line
sections.text: A phone plan can be a need for a student who studies online and a want for someone who barely uses data. A needs-vs-wants label depends on your situation, your goals and your values.

sections.heading: Three buckets work well
sections.text: Try essential (things you must pay), flexible (useful, but you can adjust the amount) and treats (things you do for joy). Treats are a healthy part of a plan when you decide on them in advance.

tips: Label each category once in Settings, then revisit it every few months.
Ask: what happens if I skip this for a month?
reflect: Which category would you never cut, even in a tight month?

quiz.q: Which statement about needs and wants is the most accurate?
options: Everyone has the same list of needs
Your needs and wants depend on your own situation
Wants are always a waste of money
quiz.why: The same purchase can be a need for one person and a want for another.

quiz.q: What is the point of a 'treats' bucket?
options: To feel guilty about fun spending
To plan enjoyment on purpose so it doesn't break your budget
quiz.why: Planned treats are sustainable. Budgets with no room for fun are the ones people abandon.

quiz.q: You can't decide if a purchase is a need. What's a useful test?
options: Ask what happens if you skip it for a month
quiz.why: Thinking through the real consequence of skipping helps separate must-haves from nice-to-haves.

title: Budgeting basics
summary: A budget is a plan for your money, not a punishment.

sections.heading: Start from your real numbers
sections.text: Look at last month's income and spending before you set limits. A limit based on what you actually spend is one you can keep.

sections.heading: Monthly limit plus category limits
sections.text: Set one overall monthly limit, then give the categories that matter most their own limit. Leave a little room for surprises.

sections.heading: A popular starting split
sections.text: The 50/30/20 idea suggests 50% essentials, 30% flexible and treats, and 20% savings. Treat it as a starting point and adapt it to your income.

tips: Review your budget once a week for five minutes.
If you often go over a limit, raise it honestly instead of ignoring it.
reflect: Which one category deserves its own budget this month?

quiz.q: Where should you start when setting a budget?
options: Your real past income and spending
quiz.why: Limits built on real data are realistic.

quiz.q: In the 50/30/20 idea, what does the 20 stand for?
quiz.why: 20% goes to savings or paying down debt.

quiz.q: You keep going over your food budget. What's a good response?
options: Check whether the limit was realistic and adjust it
quiz.why: Budgets are tools. Adjust them when real life shows they don't fit.

title: Impulse buying
summary: Pause long enough to know if you really want it.

sections.heading: Why impulses happen
sections.text: Sales banners, one-tap checkout and boredom all make buying feel urgent. The urge usually fades quickly.

sections.heading: The waiting rule
sections.text: For non-essential purchases, wait 24 hours (or 7 days for bigger ones). If you still want it afterwards, buy it guilt-free. Many urges disappear.

sections.heading: Not every impulse is bad
sections.text: Some spontaneous purchases bring real joy. The goal is awareness: notice which ones you're glad about and which you regret.

tips: Keep a wish list and review it weekly.
Mark purchases as 'impulse' in SpendWise to see your own pattern.
reflect: Think of your last impulse purchase. Are you happy you made it?

quiz.q: What does the waiting rule suggest?
quiz.why: Time between wanting and buying lets the urge fade.

quiz.q: Are all impulse purchases bad?
options: No, awareness matters more than avoidance
quiz.why: Some bring real value. Tracking helps you learn which ones you don't regret.

quiz.q: Which habit helps reduce impulse buying?
quiz.why: A wish list adds a pause before purchase.

title: Saving money
summary: Small, steady savings beat big, rare ones.

sections.heading: Pay yourself first
sections.text: Move a fixed amount to savings when money arrives, before you spend. Even ₹200 a week adds up to over ₹10,000 a year.

sections.heading: Give savings a name
sections.text: A goal like 'Laptop ₹40,000 by June' is easier to protect than a vague wish to save more. Track progress to stay motivated.

sections.heading: Automate and forget
sections.text: A fixed transfer on a fixed day removes the daily decision.

tips: Start smaller than you think you need to.
Celebrate milestones, like 25% of a goal.
reflect: What would you like to save for in the next six months?

quiz.q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
options: Save a fixed amount before spending
quiz.why: Saving first makes it automatic rather than leftover.

quiz.q: ₹200 saved every week is about how much in a year?
Why name a savings goal?
options: A specific goal is easier to protect and track
quiz.why: Specific goals keep you motivated.

title: Understanding recurring expenses
summary: Small regular payments quietly shape your whole month.

sections.heading: What counts as recurring
sections.text: Rent, phone plans, subscriptions, memberships and EMIs repeat on a schedule. Because they renew automatically, they're easy to forget.

sections.heading: Look at the yearly cost
sections.text: ₹199 a month sounds small, but it's ₹2,388 a year. Multiply by twelve to judge whether something is worth keeping.

sections.heading: Plan for them first
sections.text: Subtract recurring costs from income before deciding on flexible spending. What remains is your real freedom.

tips: List all recurring payments once and put the dates in your calendar.
reflect: Which recurring payment brings you the most value?

quiz.q: A ₹199 monthly subscription costs about how much per year?
Why are recurring payments easy to overlook?
quiz.why: Auto-renewal means no fresh decision each time.

quiz.q: What should you subtract first when planning a month?
quiz.why: Fixed commitments define how much is actually flexible.

title: Building an emergency fund
summary: A small cushion turns a crisis into an inconvenience.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text: An emergency fund is money set aside only for surprises: a medical bill, a phone repair, a sudden trip home.

sections.heading: How much
sections.text: A common target is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses. If that feels huge, start with one week of essentials, then one month.

sections.heading: Keep it separate
sections.text: Hold it in a separate account or goal so it isn't mixed with everyday spending. Refill it after you use it.

tips: Create an 'Emergency fund' goal in SpendWise and add a small amount weekly.
reflect: What are your essential expenses in a typical month?

quiz.q: An emergency fund is for…
quiz.why: It protects you from surprises.

quiz.q: A common long-term target is…
quiz.why: Three to six months of essentials gives a real cushion.

quiz.q: If a full fund feels too big, you should…
options: Start with one week of essentials
quiz.why: Small starting targets build the habit.

title: Avoiding unnecessary subscriptions
summary: Keep the ones you love, drop the ones you forgot.

sections.heading: Audit regularly
sections.text: Once a quarter, list every subscription: streaming, music, apps, cloud storage, gym. Ask when you last used each.

sections.heading: Rotate instead of stacking
sections.text: You can pause or switch streaming services month to month instead of paying for several at once.

sections.heading: Watch free trials
sections.text: Free trials often convert to paid plans. Set a reminder for a day before the trial ends.

tips: Use the 'Bills and subscriptions' category to spot repeating charges.
Share family plans where the terms allow it.
reflect: Which subscription would you miss least?

quiz.q: How often should you review subscriptions?
quiz.why: A regular audit catches forgotten charges.

quiz.q: What helps with free trials?
options: A reminder before the trial ends
quiz.why: A reminder lets you cancel before the first charge.

quiz.q: Is keeping a subscription you use and enjoy a bad choice?
options: No, value for you is what matters
quiz.why: The goal is paying for things you actually value.
